Neonatal Plains zebra (Equus quagga) typically present a wet weight at birth of 32,000 grams [Wwb = 32,000 grams], a substantial mass that reflects the highly precocial developmental strategy characteristic of equids. This large initial body size allows newborn foals to stand and follow their mothers within hours of parturition, an adaptation critical for evading predators on the open savanna. The rapid post-natal growth trajectory is supported by the nutritional composition of zebra milk, which is rich in protein and fat relative to that of many other ungulates. Field studies conducted in the Serengeti ecosystem have documented that foals gain weight at an impressive rate during the first weeks of life, driven by the energetic demands of maintaining thermoregulation and locomotion in a highly mobile herd. This substantial neonatal mass, however, represents only a fraction of the ultimate body size the animal will attain as a fully grown adult.

Adult female Plains zebra achieve an ultimate wet weight of approximately 280,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 280,000 grams], a value that places them among the medium-sized members of the genus Equus. This asymptotic body mass is typically reached by the time an individual has completed skeletal and muscular development, which generally occurs several years after the attainment of sexual maturity. In contrast, the wet weight at weaning, which marks the transition to complete nutritional independence from maternal milk, is recorded at roughly 205,000 grams [Wwx = roughly 205,000 grams]. This value indicates that a foal has more than sextupled its birth mass by the time it ceases suckling, having accumulated substantial muscle mass and fat reserves necessary for survival without maternal provisioning. Comparisons with other grazing ungulates of the African savanna suggest that this weaning mass provides a sufficient energetic buffer against seasonal fluctuations in forage quality, though the precise timing of weaning is ultimately influenced by maternal condition and the onset of the subsequent gestation.

Reproductive timing in the Plains zebra is tightly linked to the seasonality of rainfall and the consequent availability of high-quality forage. Female zebras experience a relatively extended gestation period of approximately 365 days [tg = approximately 365 days], measured at the species' stable core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This long intrauterine development phase is typical of equids and allows for the birth of a highly developed, precocial foal capable of rapid integration into the herd. The life history schedule of female Plains zebra is paced by a relatively slow maturation rate compared to other large savanna herbivores. Females reach puberty at 900 days since birth [tp = 900 days since birth], evaluated at a stable core temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C] which reflects the homeothermic condition of the species. This delayed onset of reproductive capability is a common feature among equids and is hypothesised to allow sufficient time for the attainment of critical body size and social experience necessary for successful competition within the harem structure. The maximum reproductive rate for this species, expressed as the number of offspring produced per unit time, is approximately 0.65 foals per year [Ri = approximately 0.65 foals per year] at 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], which corresponds to one foal per reproductive event [N_R_i = one foal per reproductive event] and approximately 0.65 reproductive events per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.65 reproductive events per year]. This slow reproductive pace, combined with the extended period of maternal investment, results in a low intrinsic rate of population increase that renders the species particularly vulnerable to perturbations such as drought or increased predation pressure on juveniles.

Under the species' characteristic body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], somatic maintenance and reproductive effort are integrated across the lifetime. This extended longevity is thought to be facilitated by the species' dental hypsodonty, which allows efficient mastication of abrasive grasses even as teeth wear with advancing age. Ultimately, the interplay between the 32,000 gram [Wwb = 32,000 gram] birth mass, the 205,000 gram [Wwx = 205,000 gram] weaning mass, and the 280,000 gram [Wwi = 280,000 gram] ultimate adult body mass delineates a life history strategy centred on high maternal investment in a small number of precocial offspring. This strategy, while energetically costly per offspring, confers high neonatal survival rates in an environment where predation risk is substantial and where rapid physical development is essential for integration into the protective structure of the herd.
